core.text: To say what you go *to do*, Latin has **the supine (the special purpose form after a verb of going: dormitum it = goes to sleep)**: the participle stem with -um, used after *īre*, *venīre*, *mittere* and other verbs of moving: *ambulātum exit* — he goes out to walk; *salūtātum veniō* — I come to greet you. It can take an object like a verb: *amīcum salūtātum īvit*. Latin name: *supīnum*.
English uses a plain *to* here: *he went out to walk*, *they come to watch*.
Verb of motion + supine in -um = 'to do X'. A second supine in -ū follows facilis / difficilis: facile dictū — easy to say.

invented.en: The tired boys go to sleep.

core.text: *Salūtātum* is also the neuter of **the perfect participle (the 'having been done' word: laudatus = praised)**. Ask what it is doing: after a verb of going with no noun to agree with, it is the supine ('to greet'); agreeing with a noun (*oppidum salūtātum*) it is the participle.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 22) call it the third verbal noun beside infinitive and gerund, with only two jobs: -um after motion for purpose, -ū to pin down an adjective. A deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks) forms it the same way: *venī mēcum locūtum* — come and talk with me.

Ørberg (cap. XXII) lists everyday supines: *lavātum īre*, *dormītum īre*, *cubitum īre*. Supine + *īrī* makes the rare future passive infinitive (*laudātum īrī*, cap. XXIII). For purpose in general Latin prefers *ut* + subjunctive or *ad* + gerund; the supine stays with going and sending.
